recap.text: Carl's father was a linebacker covered in tattoos who owned a stand-up Frogger machine. Carl spent hours playing the machine in the basement while his mother locked him away from his father's loud friends. On the last day they met, Carl called his father a bully, and the man laughed. He was a weekend warrior motorcycle guy who abandoned Carl twelve years ago.

Carl sees a red and beige 1965 Harley Davidson FLH Panhead Electra Glide with a dent in the gas tank. As a boy, Carl knocked the bike over and his father hit him with a belt until his underwear soaked through with blood. Carl remembers his mother attempted to kill his father and herself as a birthday present to Carl, but only half succeeded.

A sniper gnome wears a round, black half-helmet like the one Carl's father owned. After Carl's mother left, his father ripped off the helmet and smashed Carl's fish tank. The mollies flopped on the floor while Carl cut his fingers on the glass picking them up. None survived, and Carl decided never to get a pet again.

Carl finds a junkyard on a floating chunk of Iowa with his father's motorcycle and a vending machine. He watches a recording of his father in a hospital bed and tells the man he is a bully before his stepmother poisons him. Carl burns the drapes with purple flowers and takes a Glock, keys, court documents, and a Centipede cabinet. He tells Princess Donut his father does not deserve a name.

Princess Donut mentions legal papers Carl took from his father's trailer. Carl's father tried to take money his grandparents set aside for Carl. The papers include a marriage certificate and court documents from arrests.

beats.headline: Linebacker, for the record
beats.text: Crawler Carl's explanation of his own size, supplied unprompted: six foot three, about 230 pounds, and genetics. His dad was a linebacker. His mother was five foot ten, and her father played center for Oregon State before becoming a prison guard. That is the whole file at present: a position on a football team, offered as evidence. The man himself is not described at all.

beats.headline: The Frogger machine
beats.text: Two items from the file, both supplied by his son. The man was covered in tattoos, which is why Carl never wanted any. And he owned an original stand-up Frogger machine out of an arcade. When his friends came over to smoke and drink and get loud, Carl's mother locked Carl in the basement with no television, no internet, and that machine. Hours and hours of Frogger. Crawler Carl types the word into his skills search to see what happens.
beats.gist: Carl's father had tattoos and an original stand-up Frogger machine.

beats.headline: The last day Carl saw him
beats.text: Worrying about some crazy asshole with a gun, Carl is inexplicably reminded of it: the last day he ever saw his father. You're a bully, Carl told him. You're a bully and nobody likes you. It's why Mom left. Carl expected to be hit. By his own account he never had been, not once. The man laughed, and kept laughing, and that was enough. He did not need Carl to like him, he said. But Carl would respect him.
beats.gist: Carl remembers telling his father he is a bully whom nobody likes.

beats.headline: A weekend warrior
beats.text: Riding a glorified moped with his legs held off the hot sides, Carl pictures his father laughing at him and calling him a damn fool. He was a motorcycle guy. Not a full-time, leather-clad biker; more of a weekend warrior. Carl has not talked to or heard from him in over twelve years, not since the day he abandoned Carl and left him alone in the world.
beats.gist: Carl pictures his motorcycle-riding father laughing and calling him a damn fool.

beats.headline: A dent in the gas tank
beats.text: Prize four on the carousel is a 1965 Harley Davidson FLH Panhead Electra Glide, red and beige, with a small dent in the gas tank. Carl knows the dent. As a boy he slipped coming up the driveway and knocked the bike over. His father was never physically abusive, Carl says, except that day: a belt, hard enough that Carl's underwear soaked through with blood. His mother cried and said they were going back to Texas. They never went. Carl cannot tell whether it is the real motorcycle.
beats.gist: Carl sees a 1965 Harley Davidson and remembers his father hitting him with a belt.

beats.headline: Half a birthday present
beats.text: At the end of the fourth floor, with two people just gone to their deaths by their own hand, Carl thinks of his own mother. She attempted to kill his father and then herself, as a birthday present to Carl. She only half succeeded. He thinks, too, of everyone standing there with him, who jumped into certain death to save him.
beats.gist: Carl thinks of his mother attempting to kill his father and herself as a birthday present.

beats.headline: The fish tank
beats.text: A sniper gnome in a round, black half-helmet reminds Carl of his father's. Soon after Carl's mother left, a month before his father in turn left Carl to fend for himself, the man ripped that helmet off and smashed Carl's fish tank. The mollies flopped on the floor while Carl cut his fingers on the glass picking them up. None survived. Carl did not cry, and that bothered him for weeks. The lesson he took from it: never get a pet again. All they do is die.
beats.gist: A sniper gnome's helmet reminds Carl of his father, who smashed Carl's fish tank.

beats.headline: His motorcycle in an Iowa yard
beats.text: A single-wide trailer in a junkyard on a floating chunk of Iowa, and a vending machine bearing his silhouette: One Fight for Nine Tokens. Princess Donut thinks it is a fatter Carl with a mustache. In the yard stands the motorcycle, Georgia plates expired years ago, his prized possession. Carl lifts it easily, remembering how heavy it was the day he knocked it over. The yard is summer spliced into December, and along one side runs a row of alliums in pots, labelled in an elegant, feminine hand. His father would never have done that.
beats.gist: Carl finds a single-wide trailer and a vending machine of his father on a floating Iowa chunk.

beats.headline: A dying man and a remote
beats.text: He is in a hospital bed in the living room: 140 pounds, yellow skin, a patchy white beard, cursing the Mariners at the television. A small boy is sent for cigarettes: "Move, or I'll make you move, boy." His young wife, in nurse scrubs, walks past without looking at him. Zev confirms it is a recording of that day. Crawler Carl leans in, closer than he has ever been to his father's face, and tells the man who cannot hear him that he is a bully, that nobody likes him, that Carl's mother tried to kill him and his new wife is about to finish the job.
beats.gist: Carl's father is a 140-pound man with yellow skin and a patchy white beard.

beats.headline: Morphine, and the drapes
beats.text: His wife returns with a syringe and a new IV bag. "I have your medicine right here." "It's about time." "Yes," she says. "Yes, it is." Crawler Carl does not watch. From the master bedroom he hears the man say something desperate and slurred, with nobody there to hear his final words. Carl takes the Glock, the keys, a folder of court documents and a Centipede cabinet, lights one of the Marlboro Reds, and sets fire to the drapes with the purple flowers on them.
beats.gist: Carl's father dies while Carl burns drapes with purple flowers and takes a Centipede cabinet.

beats.headline: The boss he was not
beats.text: The AI's announcement: the original boss for this battle was to be Carl's deceased father, who really had three smaller creatures inside him wearing his skin like kids in a trench coat. The AI overruled that. Nine heads on the hydra instead, and his is not one of them. His voice turns up anyway, in the enemy's deck: a totem called Alpha Male Carl, Carl with gelled hair, speaks with his father's voice. Not Carl's.
beats.gist: The AI replaces Carl's father with a nine-headed hydra and a totem called Alpha Male Carl.

beats.headline: No name for him
beats.text: Crawler Carl tells Princess Donut what he saw in the trailer: his stepmother poisoned his father. Technically an overdose. Donut is confused: two different people tried to kill him? He must have been a real piece of work. She asks his name. "It doesn't matter. He doesn't deserve to have one. Not anymore." The hydra's loot hangs in the air over the burned spot where he died.
beats.gist: Carl tells Donut his stepmother poisoned his father, causing an overdose.

beats.headline: What his papers say
beats.text: Princess Donut, mid-negotiation across a table, mentions some legal papers Carl took from his father's trailer and has not read. She has. Carl's grandparents set money aside for Carl, and his father was trying to get at it without Carl knowing. A marriage certificate, for the father and his new wife. Court documents from several arrests. Together, she says, they paint a very distinct picture of who Carl's father was.
beats.gist: Donut reads legal papers from Carl's father's trailer and tells Carl his father tried to steal money.
